texts.orig: “The wedge metaphor to me is most useful in making sure you’re not a blunt instrument trying to chop into a market by being everything for everyone, but instead the sharp blade with extraordinary focus on a specific persona/use case to start.”
texts.text: “The wedge metaphor to me is most useful in making sure you’re not a blunt instrument trying to chop into a market by being everything for everyone, but instead the sharp blade with extraordinary focus on a specific persona/use case to start.”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A wedge is simply a strategy to win a large market by initially capturing (1) a tiny part of a larger market or (2) a large part of a small adjacent market.
texts.text: A wedge is simply a strategy to win a large market by initially capturing (1) a tiny part of a larger market or (2) a large part of a small adjacent market.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In business, as in rock cutting, a wedge is made up of two parts: (1) the right tool and (2) the right place to strike. In other words, the right initial product and the right initial market.
texts.text: In business, as in rock cutting, a wedge is made up of two parts: (1) the right tool and (2) the right place to strike. In other words, the right initial product and the right initial market.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Tesla’s wedge (into the larger transportation market) was a luxury car targeted at affluent early adopters. Robinhood’s wedge (into the consumer finance market) was a commission-free trading platform targeted at millennials. PayPal’s wedge (into the payments market) was an online payment platform for eBay sellers.

texts.orig: Do I always need a wedge?
texts.text: Do I always need a wedge?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: I don’t think so. Companies like Zoom, Slack, Workday, Notion, Datadog, Spotify, and Peloton went straight at their respective (large) markets with an amazing product and won. You can argue about semantics, but in practical terms, as far as I can tell, these companies didn’t use a wedge strategy—they attacked a large market straight-on.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: “We kept hearing that to enter a big market, you need a wedge—something really sharp and really specific, and then you expand from there. It turns out for some classes of problems, such as infrastructure management, which is what we do, the wedge doesn’t work. There is a large amount of stuff you need to do from day one if you want your product to be useful. Our initial product was positioned as a very broad platform to bring multiple teams together, and actually didn’t have that wedge aspect. That disconcerted some investors.”

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: When do I need a wedge?
texts.text: When do I need a wedge?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A wedge seems most essential when you’re going after a market that is (1) entrenched or (2) crowded. When it’s hard to break in head-on.
texts.text: A wedge seems most essential when you’re going after a market that is (1) entrenched or (2) crowded. When it’s hard to break in head-on.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The more entrenched and competitive the market, the more valuable a wedge will be. Chime needed a wedge to get a foothold in the entrenched banking market. Stripe needed a wedge to break into the entrenched payments market. Airbnb needed a wedge to get traction in the competitive accommodations market.
texts.text: The more entrenched and competitive the market, the more valuable a wedge will be. Chime needed a wedge to get a foothold in the entrenched banking market. Stripe needed a wedge to break into the entrenched payments market. Airbnb needed a wedge to get traction in the competitive accommodations market.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: You could certainly attempt to go at it head-on, by raising more money and building a 10x better product, but starting with a wedge has many benefits.
texts.text: You could certainly attempt to go at it head-on, by raising more money and building a 10x better product, but starting with a wedge has many benefits.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A wedge gives a startup a number of advantages over its competition—primarily driven by having a narrower, more precise focus:
texts.text: A wedge gives a startup a number of advantages over its competition—primarily driven by having a narrower, more precise focus:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: With a more focused value prop, your pitch and sales process become quicker and easier, which drives more revenue that you can reinvest in growth and the product.
texts.text: With a more focused value prop, your pitch and sales process become quicker and easier, which drives more revenue that you can reinvest in growth and the product.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: With more customers, you can more quickly build social proof (e.g. traction, logos, and testimonials).
texts.text: With more customers, you can more quickly build social proof (e.g. traction, logos, and testimonials).

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: With early revenue, you can avoid having to raise a lot of money and thus keep ownership and control longer.
texts.text: With early revenue, you can avoid having to raise a lot of money and thus keep ownership and control longer.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: You can build, launch, learn, and iterate toward product-market fit more quickly.
texts.text: You can build, launch, learn, and iterate toward product-market fit more quickly.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Once you’ve “wedged” into a company, you can expand revenue by offering additional products and services.
texts.text: Once you’ve “wedged” into a company, you can expand revenue by offering additional products and services.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “Many marketplace founders focus on the sheer size of a market. But I view too broad an initial market as a flag. I would much rather see a founder communicate a deep insight into a narrow market wedge where pull is strong. A few reasons why:
texts.text: “Many marketplace founders focus on the sheer size of a market. But I view too broad an initial market as a flag. I would much rather see a founder communicate a deep insight into a narrow market wedge where pull is strong. A few reasons why:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Liquidity is the name of the game with marketplaces. It’s faster to build liquidity in more narrowly defined market segments.
texts.text: Liquidity is the name of the game with marketplaces. It’s faster to build liquidity in more narrowly defined market segments.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Building density in one subvertical helps a team more effectively build a playbook before expanding to the next.
texts.text: Building density in one subvertical helps a team more effectively build a playbook before expanding to the next.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: The narrower the initial focus, the more likely one is to build a deeper and differentiated product.
texts.text: The narrower the initial focus, the more likely one is to build a deeper and differentiated product.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Narrower market → deeper end user empathy for founders & product teams. Conversely, too much breadth can introduce noise in early user research & product work.
texts.text: Narrower market → deeper end user empathy for founders & product teams. Conversely, too much breadth can introduce noise in early user research & product work.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Overall, starting narrow improves one's likelihood to discover & solve a precise pain point.”

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: “Wedge selection should be very intentional. Don’t just build for the first customer persona you think of or the closest city to where you live. Build for the group that has the most acute pain point, or the highest willingness to pay, or the fastest sales cycles. The more carefully you pick your wedge, the easier it will be to succeed and to expand to the larger market. A product that’s 10x better on average might actually be 50x better for some groups but only 1.1x better for others. Picking the right group will determine whether you quickly find product-market fit or face an uphill battle.”
texts.text: “Wedge selection should be very intentional. Don’t just build for the first customer persona you think of or the closest city to where you live. Picking the right group will determine whether you quickly find product-market fit or face an uphill battle.”

texts.orig: “A good example of a wedge is what I experienced seeing Gainsight’s journey from their early days when they had a few hundred thousand of ARR. They started out with a dashboard that provides a 360-degree view of each customer. With a few simple integrations—Zendesk, Salesforce, and a website tag—Gainsight would collect a trove of data about each customer and display that data in an easy-to-understand 360-degree view. This drove tremendous logo velocity for Gainsight in the early days.

With a few simple integrations—Zendesk, Salesforce, and a website tag—Gainsight would collect a trove of data about each customer and display that data in an easy-to-understand 360-degree view. texts.label: text
texts.orig: Over time, Gainsight massively expanded the product footprint to include ‘playbooks’ for CSMs (customer success managers), marketing automation (e.g. to allow CSMs to communicate with customers in an automated fashion), data science (to predict churn), etc. When Gainsight launched initially, the market wasn’t ready for this big of a transformation, but the customer-360 health score was a great wedge to help the early adopters recognize the power of building out a customer success function.
texts.text: Over time, Gainsight massively expanded the product footprint to include ‘playbooks’ for CSMs (customer success managers), marketing automation (e.g. to allow CSMs to communicate with customers in an automated fashion), data science (to predict churn), etc. When Gainsight launched initially, the market wasn’t ready for this big of a transformation, but the customer-360 health score was a great wedge to help the early adopters recognize the power of building out a customer success function.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Gainsight’s wedge worked because it was sold to the same buyer, was a fast ‘land,’ which drove lots of usage, and the footprint extension felt very natural. As a result, over time Gainsight was able to significantly increase ASPs (application service providers) from 10-15K to 30K to much, much higher over time.”

texts.orig: Our customer service rep forwarded me an email from an eBay power seller. The eBay seller had turned the PayPal logo into a nice-looking button for her auctions and was asking our permission to use it. eBay sellers were desperate for a [payments] solution because their alternative was to wait a week for a check to arrive in the mail and then wait for it to clear. Some of them had already found PayPal on their own. One of them cared enough to make an auction button and ask our permission to use it.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We rolled out other features for auction sellers that made it even more convenient to use PayPal. We dropped other plans and went all-in on the eBay use case. Results were immediate. At the end of 1999, PayPal had less than 10,000 users. By the end of January 2000, we hit 100,000 users. A few months after that, 1 million. By the summer of 2000, 5 million. It felt like the servers were melting. The growth curve looked like a perfect hockey stick.”
